interviewQuestions.question: Why is true LRU rarely implemented exactly, and what do real OSes use instead?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
True LRU needs the exact recency ordering of every resident page, and that ordering has to be updated on every single memory reference — either a timestamp write per access or a linked-list reordering per access. At the frequency memory gets accessed, that overhead would slow down every access just to make eviction marginally better, which is a terrible trade for something that only matters when memory is actually full.

Real kernels use the clock (second-chance) algorithm instead: hardware sets a single reference bit for free whenever a page is touched, and the replacement algorithm only has to look at that bit lazily, at eviction time, sweeping through resident pages and giving any page with its bit set a second chance before evicting it. This gets most of LRU's fault-rate quality — because pages that are genuinely being used keep getting their bit re-set before the hand comes back around — at a cost barely above FIFO's.

I'd go a step further for a staff-level answer: production kernels like Linux don't even stop at plain clock — they run a multi-list active/inactive LRU approximation, and treat file-backed pages (cheap to evict, just re-read from disk) differently from anonymous pages (must go to swap). The theme across all of this is the same: approximate the expensive, precise policy with something hardware can support almost for free.

**Testing:** whether you can name the actual cost of true LRU and the actual mechanism (reference bit, not just 'a cheaper version') real systems substitute.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why LRU is approximated, not exact

interviewQuestions.question: What is Belady's Anomaly, and why does it not happen under LRU?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Belady's Anomaly is the counterintuitive result that, under FIFO replacement specifically, giving a system *more* physical frames can *increase* the total number of page faults for the same reference string — the opposite of what intuition says extra memory should do. The classic textbook example (reference string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5) produces 9 faults with 3 frames but 10 with 4 frames under FIFO.

The root cause is that FIFO's eviction order depends purely on load time, and adding a frame changes which pages get evicted and when in a way that isn't guaranteed to only help — the set of pages resident at any point under 4 frames isn't a strict superset of the set under 3 frames.

LRU (and Optimal) avoid this because they have the **stack property**: the set of pages that would be resident with N frames is always a subset of the set resident with N+1 frames, at every point in the reference string, for algorithms built this way. That guarantee mathematically rules out the anomaly — more frames can never leave you worse off. I'd close by noting this is a genuine, provable reason to prefer LRU-family algorithms beyond just 'it approximates optimal better' — it also behaves *monotonically*, which FIFO simply doesn't.

**Testing:** whether you know the mechanism behind the anomaly (stack property) rather than just being able to name the phenomenon.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Belady's Anomaly and the stack property

interviewQuestions.question: Walk through why the clock algorithm is considered a good practical compromise between FIFO and LRU.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
FIFO is cheap (a queue, no per-access cost) but ignores usage entirely, so it can evict a page that's actively being used just because it happened to load early. True LRU tracks usage precisely but needs bookkeeping on every single memory access, which is too expensive to run at memory speed. Clock sits between them by using information that's already nearly free: a single reference bit per page, set automatically by hardware whenever the page is touched, with zero extra cost on the access path itself.

At eviction time, the algorithm walks a circular list of resident pages; a page with its bit set gets a second chance (bit cleared, move on) rather than being evicted outright, and only a page that's survived a full sweep without being re-touched actually gets evicted. This means pages under active use — which keep getting their bit re-set by ordinary access — effectively never come up as the chosen victim, closely mirroring what true LRU would decide, without paying LRU's per-access tax.

The honest caveat I'd add: clock isn't identical to LRU — it can occasionally make a slightly worse choice than exact LRU would, and its accuracy depends on how the hand's sweep rate compares to the access rate. But in every real system this is measured against, the fault-rate gap versus true LRU is small, while the implementation cost gap is enormous — which is exactly the trade production kernels take.

**Testing:** whether you understand clock as a deliberate cost/accuracy trade-off, not just a black-box algorithm to memorize.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Clock as FIFO/LRU compromise
